Chapter 8: Wrestling with Culture, Politics, and the Temptation of Tribalism.
You know, the world’s full of lines—us and them, right and wrong, who’s in, and who’s out. It’s just so easy to get pulled into that need to belong, to find safety in a group, and to start drawing boundaries that keep others at arm’s length. For a lot of people, faith becomes another badge—just one more way to show who’s part of the group and who isn’t.
Picture this—a college student, fired up about justice, suddenly finds herself torn between competing loyalties. Her faith community expects her to vote a certain way, to stick to certain opinions, even to avoid certain people. Meanwhile, her friendships are pulling her in other directions. It’s exhausting. She starts to wonder—can you really belong without turning your back on who you are?
Here’s something most of us don’t realize: our beliefs? They’re shaped way more by the culture around us than we think. The news, social media, friends, family—all of it creates this echo chamber. It just keeps reinforcing what we already believe, and makes it even tougher to see the humanity in people who think differently.
Imagine one evening around a dinner table. Suddenly, a heated conversation erupts. Voices get loud, tempers flare, and for a moment, it feels like the room might split right down the middle. But then, someone takes a breath and quietly asks, “What are you afraid of?” Just like that, the mood changes. The conversation shifts from accusation to curiosity, from being defensive to actually trying to understand.
It’s pretty clear—the pull of tribalism is strong. Most of us just want to feel safe, to know who’s on our side, and to avoid the discomfort of disagreement. But real faith asks for something deeper. It calls us to listen, to learn, and, maybe hardest of all, to love even those who seem impossible to love.
There’s this man—he grew up seeing the world in black and white. But then he starts spending time with people who are nothing like him. Different backgrounds, beliefs, stories. At first? It’s uncomfortable. But slowly, he discovers a richness he never expected. The world starts to feel bigger, more complex, and honestly, more beautiful.
Over time, that urge to draw lines begins to fade. In its place, there’s a new kind of humility—a sense that none of us has all the answers, and that we all need grace. You start to see that faith isn’t about building walls. It’s about building bridges. It’s about recognizing the image of God in every person, even those who seem most different from you.
